terms.latin: vicis, vicem, vice; pl. vicēs, vicibus f.
terms.gloss: a turn; one’s turn in a succession
terms.grammar: noun, third declension, no nominative singular
terms.comment: Change, succession, one’s turn (Lewis & Short); a shift is said through the turns: in vicem or per vicēs labōrāre, to work in shifts. The accusative vicem with a genitive or a possessive also means “instead of” or “on account of” (erī vicem meamque, Plaut. Capt. 3.3.11, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Caes. BG 7.85.5: dēfatīgātīs in vicem integrī succēdunt (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Caesar’s word for troops relieving each other; not in Cicero, who says vicissim (Lewis & Short). See in turn.

evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.4.93: noctū vigiliās agere ad aedēs sacrās (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: One of the four watches into which the Romans divided the night, and the men who kept it: for a night shift of guards or nurses. Tertiā vigiliā, in the third watch, after midnight.

phrases.english: fresh men take over from the tired, shift by shift

phrases.latin: hī rursus in vicem annō post in armīs sunt, illī domī remanent
phrases.english: these in their turn are under arms the year after, and the others stay at home

sources: Lewis & Short: vicis · Lewis & Short: invicem · Lewis & Short: vigilia
